faqs.a: Under 20% is comfortable — debt is a small slice of your income. 20–35% is manageable but leaves little slack. Above 35% is risky: one emergency can tip you over. Above 43%, most mortgage lenders will hesitate.
faqs.q: What is a good debt ratio?

faqs.a: This is the quick version: one total for debts, one total for income. The full DTI calculator itemizes each debt type (housing, car, cards) and shows front-end vs back-end ratios, which is what mortgage lenders actually use.
faqs.q: How is this different from the debt-to-income ratio calculator?

faqs.a: Lenders use gross (before tax) income, so this calculator does too — it keeps you comparable to lending standards. But run it once with take-home pay as well; if that number scares you, trust the scarier one.
faqs.q: Should I use gross or net income?

faqs.a: Stop new borrowing immediately, list every debt by rate, and attack the highest-rate balance first (or use the debt payoff calculator). A 45% ratio means nearly half your income is pre-spent — that is an emergency, not a lifestyle.
No. Zero debt is a strength, not unused capacity. Borrow only for things that grow in value or earning power — education, a home you can afford, a business — never to fund consumption.
faqs.q: Does a 0% ratio mean I should borrow more?

faqs.a: Monthly, right after payday. It takes seconds, and the trend matters more than any single reading: a ratio falling 2 points a quarter means your plan is working.

debt-ratio-calculator.formula:
Debt ratio = (total monthly debt payments / gross monthly income) x 100.
Example: 18,000 / 60,000 x 100 = 30%.
howTo: Add up every monthly debt payment: EMIs, card minimums, loans.
Enter your gross monthly income (before tax).
Read your ratio and the verdict instantly.
For a detailed breakdown by debt type, try the full DTI calculator.
keyFacts: Debt ratio = total monthly debt payments ÷ gross monthly income × 100.
It is the simplified cousin of the full debt-to-income ratio — one number, no itemizing.
Lenders watch this number closely; above 43% most mortgages get difficult.
It ignores savings, assets, and expenses — it measures debt load only.
A falling ratio over time is one of the clearest signs your finances are healing.

debt-ratio-calculator.quickAnswer: If you pay ₹18,000 a month toward debts and earn ₹60,000, your debt ratio is 30% — in the manageable zone, but with little room for new borrowing. Under 20% is comfortable, 20–35% is workable, and above 35% means debt is starting to run your budget.
debt-ratio-calculator.tagline: One quick number that shows how much of your income goes to debt each month.
debt-ratio-calculator.workedExample:
Monthly debt payments ₹18,000, gross monthly income ₹60,000:
1. Ratio = 18,000 / 60,000 = 0.30.
2. As a percentage: 0.30 x 100 = 30%.
3. Verdict: 30% falls in the 20–35% manageable band — okay for now, but avoid new debt until it drops under 20%.
